item.title: Belonging to Humanity
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Belonging to Humanity

Global belonging against war and division.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Global belonging means experiencing ourselves as an integral part of the Earth.
  • Belonging to one group can come at the cost of other people’s safety and belonging.
  • A sense of global belonging may encourage care for the planet and our fellow humans.
  • Feeling part of the Earth need not displace belonging to a nation, culture, or community.

Maybe our sense of global belonging is a matter of perspective. Zoom out, and a viewer might see something as complex as a sprawling ant colony: humans building infrastructure and working collectively, laying foundations for homes where they hope to live safely on the singular haven we call Earth, spinning on its axis in a cold, heedless universe. Inhabitants must surely be united in the protection of one another on the planet they share.

But zoom back in, and our viewer might be shocked to see violence directed at people because of where they live and the destruction of homes, schools, and communities: people killing other people.

It's all about perspective.

For much of history, humans lived in small groups, as families, clans, and tribes. The need for a sense of global belonging may have been less apparent to people who lived their lives close to their birthplaces. Pre-industrial humans had limited impact on their planetary home and its inhabitants. Still, a sense of global belonging was probably high for people exposed daily to both the providence and the cruel indifference of their earthly surroundings. Earth was a protector and a threat, and living disconnected from it was not an option.

Looking back, though, we see long histories of belonging disruption, displacement, and dispossession. Modern society’s issues with belonging are not new. Belonging to one group can mean believing we must destroy another. In my chapter, “Global Belonging: From Conflict and Exclusion to Untapped Potential,” I describe such tension: “Conflicts and violence of this nature could arise from individuals who feel a strong sense of belonging rather than those who lack it, as one might assume” (Allen, 2026, pp. 235–236).

Feeling Ourselves as Part of the Earth

Those of us who study belonging cannot always assume that strengthening belonging within a group will make people’s lives better, safer, or happier. We tend to study belonging in dyads and triads, in groups and organisations. But what if we consider our collective home, Earth? Does sharing a planet mean feeling that we all belong to it?

Global belonging means experiencing ourselves as an integral part of the Earth. It is the feeling that Earth is somewhere we belong. A sense of belonging to the Earth should encourage care for the planet and our fellow humans. It should help engender concern for others’ safety and belonging, even when our own remains unthreatened.

Feeling part of the Earth need not displace belonging to a nation, culture, or community. These attachments remain important. But the atmosphere does not care where the carbon dioxide came from. At an existential level, we must strengthen our sense of global belonging, regardless of what those preaching fracture and disruption would have us believe. Our very survival depends on it.

The Overview Effect

Zoom out again, this time far enough to see the Earth as a whole. Astronauts describe feeling more connected to the Earth and its inhabitants after viewing the planet from space. These connections offer a way to imagine the planet as somewhere we all belong. My chapter describes this change in perspective: “This cognitive shift, termed the Overview Effect by Frank White in 1987 based on his interviews with astronauts, describes the awareness that emerges from viewing Earth as a shared home” (Allen, 2026, p. 242). This experience is linked to changes in values, environmental concerns and behaviours, and identification with humanity as a whole and with the planet.

We do not know whether this type of belonging can be encouraged in everyday life, or whether it creates an enduring sense of global belonging. Researchers will need to examine if global belonging influences the choices we make, particularly in times of war, conflict, and suffering.

Our belonging to family, culture, and country can coexist with the understanding that those outside these constructs also belong to our shared humanity. Exclusionary nationalism, for instance, often comes at the cost of ignoring how others can belong in the same spaces. We do not need everyone to agree or share the same political beliefs. From above, we might still look like a collective, cohesive ant colony, but zooming in reveals people whose global belonging is not only threatened but annihilated. What could the world look like if we cared enough for humanity not to destroy our world or the people in it? And would that not be the type of world most of us would want to live in?

item.title: Toxic Relatives: Where to Draw the Line for Your Kids?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Toxic Relatives: Where to Draw the Line for Your Kids?

You want your children to know their family. You also want them to be safe.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Deciding how much contact your children have with toxic relatives can be difficult.
  • Assess whether your concern involves your children’s safety or differences in parenting preferences.
  • Look for family allies who will respect your boundaries and act if a problem arises.
A mother has a protective hand on her son's shoulder as the family gathers in the background.
Source: AI-Generated

“They should see it. It’s good for them.”

Some dysfunctional families believe that children need to learn about and be exposed to what they call “real life.” Perhaps, as children, the adults weren’t protected from family chaos and believe everyone should have the same experiences. Maybe they think it will make the children tougher. Or maybe the problematic behaviors are so normalized that they seem like no big deal.

When family members choose to move away from the dysfunction, literally or figuratively, another question may come later: How much should they expose their own children to?

In healthy families, relatives will generally respect each other’s parenting choices. This includes everything from dietary restrictions and screen time to values and disciplinary practices. They may not agree with the parents’ approach, but they accept the rules. They understand that it is up to them to make the best decisions for their children.

In toxic families, relatives may disregard these rules. They may see little to no harm in exposing children to the patterns that make the family toxic in the first place. They may not value rules and structure or see the problem in putting children in compromising positions with behaviors and activities that are not age-appropriate. It may go as far as exposing children to unsafe or abusive adults, violence, and substance abuse.

That is not to say that the negative exposure is always intentional. Some relatives may be so accustomed to the chaos that they are unable to recognize that anything is wrong. However, others may see it as a necessary life lesson for their “sheltered” younger relatives.

Regardless of the intention, it does not eliminate the potential impact on children.

It is pertinent to protect children from dangers such as unsecured firearms, abusive relatives, or substance misuse. Other situations may leave parents with ambiguity about what to do.

You may value family time and want your children to have a relationship with their relatives. However, you may have your own boundaries about how much time you want them to spend with your family and the nature of that time. Choosing this for your children can be complicated.

Keep in mind that having some flexibility is good for kids. Resilient children have fewer behavioral problems, higher social functioning, and better academic outcomes later in life.1

Questions to Ask Yourself

What am I protecting my children from?

Be specific in your answer. Are you worried about their physical or emotional safety? If safety is on the line, there is no question. Protecting your children is the priority, even when enforcing that decision is difficult.

Is it a difference in parenting preferences?

Time with cousins who may have fewer restrictions on screen time or later bedtimes may be frustrating, but is unlikely to cause long-term harm. You can address an occasional disruption to your routine when you return home.

If you experienced childhood trauma, it may be tempting to fall into black-and-white thinking, but decisions do not have to be all or nothing. Get creative. Maybe it’s a daytime visit with cousins without the sleepover.

Are there safe adults around?

The only safe adult may be you or your spouse, but sometimes there are other relatives that are willing and ready to step into the gap. There may be circumstances where you are forced to leave your children with relatives. Are there other people in the family who will respect your limits and look out for your children? Will they agree with you privately but be able to stand up to problematic relatives?

Look to someone who is not afraid to hold the line when another family member objects. Lean on the person who will follow through and call you when a problem arises.

How do my children respond to these visits?

When you expose your children to your dysfunctional family, how do they respond? Are they confused and question the behaviors? Do they know your household values and where things deviate?

Listen to your child’s report of interactions that may have made them uncomfortable. Do they describe being afraid, teased, pressured, or told to keep secrets? Or did they have a positive, enjoyable time?

Your child’s experience may not mirror your own. Some toxic parents may mature and grow into stable grandparents. Others don’t and sustain the same problematic and abusive habits.

Are you looking at your family through wounded eyes? Or has the environment changed enough for you to feel secure in bringing your children around?

Different Strokes for Different Folks

You do not have to decide about every relative or every gathering all at once. You can make those decisions on a case-by-case basis. As a parent, you have the right to decide who your child spends time with, for how long, and under what circumstances. It is all right to discuss and hear out your family’s perspective, but it is ultimately up to you.

Relatives don’t have to like your boundaries, but they should respect them. This is how you break the cycle and keep chaos from passing to the next generation.
